newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish workers hit streets to protest wage freeze.
newsitem.headline: Spanish workers hit streets to protest wage freeze.

text.p: Spanish workers took to the streets on Tuesday to protest against a freeze on public-sector wages intended to help whip the country's finances into shape for Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU).

Thousands of workers who stand to be affected by the freeze demonstrated in Madrid and regional capitals on Tuesday evening in the largest mass protest since the Popular Party (PP) came to power in May.
Labour leaders vowed to keep fighting against the measure and said they were ready for a general strike before the end of the year if the government refused to back down.

"If the government continues with this attitude...we will have to move towards other measures...like a strike of the entire sector," said Antonio Gutierrez, secretary general of Workers' Commissions (CCOO), one of Spain's two largest unions.
Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato said: "This is a decision which the government has taken and which is not going to change."

With the ink still wet on a pensions deal between the unions and the new conservative administration, the protest shows unions are involved in an uneasy love-hate relationship with the government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar.
They have succeeded in striking a deal guaranteeing the purchasing power and future payment of pensions which employers' organisations denounced as over-generous and refused to sign.
But they are digging in their heels on a wage freeze the government calls irreversible.

The unions, led by CCOO and the General Workers' Union (UGT), say the measure violates an agreement with the previous Socialist administration which guaranteed wages would rise in line with inflation in 1997.
Public-sector workers have lost 11.2 percent of their buying power since 1993, saving the government 785 billion pesetas ($6 billion) in the process, according to the labour leaders.
"We're wondering what sacrifices they are asking of capital and company taxes," said Domingo Fernandez of the Confederation of Independent and Public Sector Unions (CSI-CSIF).
"We can't see any. On the contrary, they are granting them around half a trillion pesetas in capital gains," he added.
The government says the wage freeze is needed as part of an austere 1997 draft budget aimed at bringing Spain's deficit down to the level required to join EMU in 1999.

It estimates the measure will slash 200 billion pesetas ($1.5 billion) off the deficit, helping to bring it down to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from a forecast 4.4 percent in 1996.

Shortly after taking office, Aznar said his priority was to reach a German-style jobs pact with unions to tackle Spain's unemployment rate of almost 23 percent. Early talks with unions and employers failed and the issue was put on the back-burner.

Future talks will now have to overcome employers' irritation over pensions talks, while financial markets would frown on the government giving in to unions on key issues such as making it cheaper to fire workers.
